app_claim: Grime’s Graves phase: “Deep flint mines being dug” from -2600 to -2101, size 4. Summary: “A field of more than 400 late Neolithic flint mine shafts in the Norfolk Breckland, worked from about 2600 to about 2100 BCE.”
problem: The app turns a much later, brief resumption of mining into roughly 500 years of continuous deep mining. The 2018 radiocarbon modelling says the deep galleried shafts were worked probably from the third quarter of the 27th century cal BCE and ended in the decades around 2400 cal BCE; after a c.500-year gap, mining resumed briefly in the middle 16th to middle 15th centuries cal BCE.

evidence.title: When and Why? The Chronology and Context of Flint Mining at Grime’s Graves, Norfolk, England
evidence.publisher: Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society / Cambridge University Press
evidence.what_it_says: “The deepest, most complex galleried shafts were worked probably from the third quarter of the 27th century cal bc … Their use ended in the decades around 2400 cal bc … After a gap of around half a millennium, flint mining at Grime’s Graves briefly resumed, probably from the middle of the 16th century cal bc to the middle of the 15th.”

new_values.$[12].phases[0].label: Deep galleried flint mines being worked
new_values.$[12].summary: A field of more than 400 late Neolithic flint mine shafts in the Norfolk Breckland. The deep galleried shafts were probably worked from the third quarter of the 27th century to around 2400 BCE; after a gap of about half a millennium, mining briefly resumed in the 16th to 15th centuries BCE.
new_values.$[12].phases[1].label: Mines disused; later Bronze Age pit digging, then middens and a settlement from about 1400 BCE

app_claim: Dover: “Dubris, base of the Classis Britannica, with twin lighthouses” from 117 to 270, then “Saxon Shore fort” from 271 to 410.
problem: The continuous Classis Britannica phase continues through the period when English Heritage says that fort was demolished around AD 215 and a new fort was constructed around AD 270. The app therefore omits the demolition and makes the Saxon Shore fort start only one year after the new construction. Its 117 start is also more precise than the source’s “seventy years after the Roman invasion in AD 43”.

evidence.title: History of Dover Castle
evidence.what_it_says: “Seventy years after the Roman invasion in AD 43, construction of a fort began at the mouth of the river Dour. This was Dubris, a fort for the classis Britannica… it began again around AD 130 and the fort was completed.” It continues: “The fort at Dubris was demolished around AD 215 and a new one constructed around AD 270.”

new_values.$[55].summary: The shortest crossing to Gaul. A Roman fort and port at Dubris began seventy years after the invasion; the Classis Britannica fort was completed around AD 130, demolished around 215, and a new shore fort was built around 270. The Roman lighthouse still stands inside the castle, whose great tower Henry II built in 1179–89.

problem: The blanket “Deserted” label contradicts the same entry’s own uncertainty note and English Heritage: a chapel stood on the headland by about AD 1000. The phase should say that the recorded settlement was sparse while preserving the chapel evidence rather than claiming total desertion for over seven centuries.

evidence.title: History of Scarborough Castle
evidence.what_it_says: English Heritage dates the Roman signal station to the late 4th century, says a chapel stood on the headland by about AD 1000, and dates the castle probably to the 1130s.

new_values.$[124].phases[1].label: Headland with little recorded occupation; a chapel by about AD 1000
new_values.$[124].phases[1].note: The word ‘deserted’ was too strong: English Heritage records a chapel on the headland by about AD 1000, before the castle of the 1130s.
new_values.$[124].summary: A late 4th-century Roman signal station on a headland that later held a chapel by about AD 1000 and a major royal castle from the 1130s.
